# Common learning sequence

Write from the researcher's question to the defensible result:
**question → design → data → method → assumptions → output → clinical meaning → reporting**.

| Component | The chapter must establish |
|:----------|:---------------------------|
| Question | Population, comparison or relationship, time point, and target quantity |
| Design | Sampling, assignment, unit, independence, pairing, or clustering |
| Data | Variable roles, scales, units, coding, missingness, and analysis set |
| Method | Why the procedure answers the specified question |
| Assumptions | Which conditions matter, how they are assessed, and what alternatives mean |
| Output | Estimate, uncertainty, sample size, direction, denominator, and reference category |
| Clinical meaning | Magnitude in context, uncertainty, and the design's interpretation limits |
| Reporting | A reproducible methods description and a clear results statement |

## Chapter pattern

Begin with learning objectives and a health question. Explain the method in
plain language before using notation. Define each equation's symbols and
conditions. Include a small calculated illustration where useful, a reporting
example, common errors, and review questions with answers.

Give Hands-on its own subsection and note callout. The current review version
leaves this box empty for author-supplied datasets and screenshots. Do not leave
other teaching sections as heading-only placeholders. Do not fill the reserved
box with fabricated software output.

## Series boundaries

Volume I describes, compares, associates, and reports. Its regression chapters
are introductory, with one predictor. Volume II adjusts and develops specialist
models, with diagnostics and clear interpretation. Volume III assesses advanced
validity, extends dependence structures, validates prediction, synthesises
evidence, and develops the jamovi–R record.

An introductory mention is not a promise of a complete procedure. Clearly refer
readers to the later volume when the design requires a method beyond the present
chapter. Keep reliability, agreement, diagnostic accuracy, prediction, and causal
inference as distinct targets.

## Review standards

Check numerical examples independently. Keep group order, units, interval
method, and p-value convention consistent between tables, text, and figures.
Interpret a non-significant result using its uncertainty rather than declaring
equality. Do not describe an unadjusted association as a causal effect or an
in-sample fit statistic as evidence of validated clinical prediction.

Use official software documentation and primary methodological or reporting
sources. Cite them beside the relevant explanation. The source register provides
an inspectable record. Record jamovi and module versions in each practical case.
Read both rendered formats after adding figures, tables, or long callouts.

Use simple formal academic prose, informative headings, and a consistent author
and series title. All current health examples are explicitly invented; replace
that label only when a documented dataset actually supports the reported result.
